newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soyproduct offer drops amid record exports.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soyproduct offer drops amid record exports.

text.p: Brazil's supply of soyoil and soymeal has dried up as most of its domestic soybean production has been exported, leaving little for crushers, traders said.

"It's a combination of this year's more aggressive sales, with less available for the domestic industry," said Fabio Triguerinho, secretary general of the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove).
"It naturally means that the volumes available from now on will be lower than what Brazil normally has," he added.
Soybean stocks stood at 12.6 million tonnes on July 1, down from 13.5 million tonnes at the same time last year, independent consultants Safas e Mercado calculated in their latest report.

With 84 percent of this year's harvest committed by end-June, the internal market was already showing the shortages characteristic of the gap in between harvests, with local supply totally dependent on imports, it added.
Following the recent sharp drops in Chicago futures, producers are going to be less keen to sell what little product they have left, traders said.
In concrete terms, what this means is that "you're not going to be able to buy 300,000 tonnes in two days," said one soymeal trader.
He said supply levels would rise again after the arrival of imports of U.S. new crop soybeans between October and December.
But until then any potential buyers, such as China, may have to look to the U.S. to fill their needs, one broker said.
Traders were divided about the level of Chinese interest in recent weeks, with some saying they had not heard of any enquiries for a while.
"I think they were in the market but we didn't do anything with them," said a sales director at a large processor.
He added that because of a recent rise in U.S. premiums, the U.S. was now just as competitive as Brazil as a supplier of soyoil.
"For soyoil, up until 15 to 20 days ago, the U.S. was not competitive," he said. "The premiums rose and made the U.S. competitive again."
Traders said the drop in international prices raised the spectre of cancellations, but pointed out that this was always a risk, not just at current market conditions.
"It's a risk, but it hasn't happened until now and I don't see why it suddenly should," said the soymeal trader.
